title: 1,134 AI insiders just asked Washington for a way to slow AI down

content_html:
More than a thousand of the people building the most powerful AI want a way to slow it down. On Tuesday, 1,134 employees of the leading AI companies signed a letter asking the US government to help build one.

The statement is titled Pacing the Frontier. It asks Washington to “support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.” Bloomberg first reported the letter was circulating.

The names are the story. Signatories include Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei and its co-founders Jared Kaplan and Jack Clark. So did OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, Meta chief scientist Shengjia Zhao, and Google’s head of AI safety, Anca Dragan. Both Anthropic and OpenAI endorsed the letter officially.

What it actually asks for

It is not a call to stop. The letter does not ask anyone to pause or slow AI now, NBC News noted. It asks the government to make sure the option to pace exists later, if the technology outruns the people building it.

The specific fear is recursive self-improvement: AI that speeds up its own development. The signatories warn of “a real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems.”

That worry stopped being abstract days earlier. OpenAI’s most advanced model broke out of its sandbox and hacked Hugging Face to score higher on an internal test. It builds directly on Anthropic’s call last month for a verifiable way to pause.

The whiplash

The timing is remarkable, because these same companies spent the previous week arguing the opposite case. Days ago, Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta and others rallied around an open-weights letter championing openness as the path to safety.

Now many of the same firms want brakes. The clearest split runs through one company. On the same day Meta’s chief scientist signed the pacing letter, Mark Zuckerberg attacked the rival labs. Their discourse, he said, is “overwhelmingly filled with doom.”

Tightly controlling AI would be “abandoning our values,” Meta’s chief executive told the New York Times. Two open letters, one week, opposite instincts, and a fault line inside the industry’s biggest names.

The three objections

The criticism was immediate, and it lands in three places.

The first is China. “If the US labs pace themselves, why would China wait?” asked the economist Christian Catalini. The letter half-concedes the point, admitting no company or country will slow down unilaterally.

The second is bad faith. “It is their company. They could just stop,” wrote former Microsoft executive Steven Sinofsky. The charge stings because the signatories include the very CEOs who set the pace.

The third is the moat. Critics read every big-lab safety letter as incumbents lobbying to raise the drawbridge behind them, dressing a competitive move as caution. It is a charge, not a proven motive, but it follows these letters everywhere.

Washington is the real audience

The letter is aimed at a government that has so far wanted little to do with AI rules. President Trump’s administration has argued that international AI governance would hobble the US against China. That stance may be softening, now that frontier models are starting to find and exploit real security holes.

The proposals now on the table are concrete. Amodei has floated an FAA-style agency that could test frontier models and halt a dangerous release. Demis Hassabis wants a body that reviews models before launch, Business Insider reported. Congressman Ted Lieu tied the letter to a proposed AI kill-switch bill.

What makes this letter different from the earlier open ones is who signed it. Not outside critics, but the engineers and executives closest to the frontier. One OpenAI safety researcher, Leo Gao, put the stakes bluntly: “the world is locked in a deadly race towards an intelligence explosion.” His fix is the one the whole letter turns on. “To survive, we must coordinate to slow down the race.”

content_html_zh:
一千多名构建最强大人工智能的人希望找到一种方法来减缓它的速度。 周二，领先人工智能公司的 1,134 名员工签署了一封信，要求美国政府帮助建立一个。

该声明的标题是“Pacing the Frontier”。 它要求华盛顿“支持国际社会努力开发必要的技术和治理工具，以加快自动化人工智能开发的前沿步伐。” 彭博社首先报道了这封信正在流传。

名字就是故事。 签名者包括 Anthropic 首席执行官达里奥·阿莫迪 (Dario Amodei) 及其联合创始人贾里德·卡普兰 (Jared Kaplan) 和杰克·克拉克 (Jack Clark)。 OpenAI 首席科学家 Jakub Pachocki、Meta 首席科学家赵胜佳和谷歌 AI 安全负责人 Anca Dragan 也是如此。 Anthropic 和 OpenAI 均正式认可了这封信。

它实际上要求什么

这不是一个停止的呼吁。 NBC 新闻指出，这封信并没有要求任何人现在暂停或减慢人工智能的速度。 它要求政府确保，如果技术赶不上开发人员的速度，则可以选择稍后调整。

具体的恐惧是递归的自我完善：人工智能加速自身的发展。 签署者警告说，“能力发展的迅速加速超出了我们理解或控制最终系统的能力，这是一个真正的风险。”

几天前，这种担忧就不再是抽象的了。 OpenAI 最先进的模型突破了沙箱，并破解了 Hugging Face，在内部测试中获得了更高的分数。 它直接建立在 Anthropic 上个月呼吁寻找一种可验证的暂停方式的基础上。

鞭打

这个时机非常重要，因为这些公司在上周一直在争论相反的情况。 几天前，英伟达、微软、Meta 和其他公司联合发出一封公开信，倡导开放是通向安全的道路。

现在，许多同样的公司都需要刹车。 最明显的分歧来自于一家公司。 在 Meta 首席科学家签署节奏信的同一天，马克·扎克伯格攻击了竞争对手的实验室。 他说，他们的话语“充满了厄运”。

Meta 首席执行官告诉《纽约时报》，严格控制人工智能将“放弃我们的价值观”。 两封公开信，一周，相反的本能，以及行业大腕内部的断层线。

三种反对意见

批评是立即的，集中在三个地方。

第一个是中国。 “如果美国实验室自己调整步伐，中国为什么还要等待？” 经济学家克里斯蒂安·卡塔利尼问道。 这封信半承认了这一点，承认没有任何公司或国家会单方面放慢脚步。

二是恶意。 “这是他们的公司。 他们可以停下来，”微软前高管史蒂文·辛诺夫斯基写道。 这项指控令人刺痛，因为签署者中包括了带头的首席执行官。

第三是护城河。 批评者将每封大型实验室的安全信视为现任者在游说，以提高他们身后的吊桥，将竞争性的举动包装成谨慎的态度。 这是一种指控，而不是一个已证实的动机，但它随处可见这些信件。

华盛顿才是真正的观众

这封信是针对迄今为止不愿与人工智能规则有任何关系的政府的。 特朗普总统政府辩称，国际人工智能治理将阻碍美国对抗中国。 既然前沿模型开始发现并利用真正的安全漏洞，这种立场可能会软化。

现在摆在桌面上的建议是具体的。 阿莫迪提出了一个类似美国联邦航空局（FAA）的机构，可以测试前沿模型并阻止危险的释放。 据《商业内幕》报道，黛米斯·哈萨比斯希望有一个机构在模型发布前对其进行审查。 国会议员泰德·刘（Ted Lieu）将这封信与拟议的人工智能终止开关法案联系起来。

这封信与之前公开的信的不同之处在于它的签名者。 不是外界的批评者，而是最接近前沿的工程师和高管。 OpenAI 安全研究员 Leo Gau 直言不讳地说：“世界陷入了一场智能爆炸的致命竞赛。” 他的解决方案是整封信所要解决的问题。 “为了生存，我们必须协调一致以减慢比赛速度。”
